rc-s001.x: In one study of mustard and sunflower farms, researchers counted the insects that visited flowers each day. Honeybees were the most numerous visitors, but they were far from the only ones. Solitary bees, hoverflies and even beetles also carried pollen from plant to plant. Honeybees tended to work the same few plants again and again, which limited how far pollen travelled. Wild visitors moved more erratically, and this wandering helped to mix pollen from many different plants. The fields with the greatest variety of insects produced the heaviest seed crops, even where the number of honeybee hives was the same. The researchers do not suggest that beekeeping should be abandoned. Their point is that farmers who clear hedgerows and spray flowering margins may be removing the very helpers that raise their yields. Leaving a strip of wild flowers beside the crop costs little land, and it gives wild insects food and shelter between harvests.

rc-s002.x: The ruins of Mohenjo-daro, in Sindh, show that its builders cared a great deal about everyday cleanliness. Many houses had a bathing area, and waste water ran from it into small drains built of baked brick. These joined larger covered drains that ran beneath the main streets, and removable bricks allowed workers to clear blockages. A visitor today can still trace these channels in the brickwork. Such planning suggests more than skill with bricks. It suggests that someone organised the work, that households were expected to follow common rules, and that the drains were maintained after they were built. A drain is useful only if it is kept clear, and the long life of these structures points to regular care. Archaeologists are careful, however, about guessing how the city was governed. The drains tell us what people built, not who gave the orders. Other questions, such as who lived in each house, must be answered by different kinds of evidence.

rc-s003.x: When the Nawaz family moved to a new neighbourhood in Lahore, their daughter Hira was unhappy about leaving her old school and friends. Her mother noticed a small lending library at the end of the street, run by retired teachers from a rented room. Members paid a small monthly fee and could borrow two books at a time. Hira joined reluctantly and chose a book of short stories only because the cover was bright. Within a month she was visiting twice a week. The librarians soon learned her taste and began leaving suitable books on a shelf for her. They also started a weekly reading hour, where children read aloud to one another. Hira's confidence grew, and so did her marks in English. The library never held many books and its furniture was old, but it offered something larger shelves cannot: people who knew what each reader needed. Her mother later said that the fee was the best money the family had ever spent.

rc-s004.x: Inflation is often described as a rise in the general level of prices, but its effects are felt unevenly. A family that spends most of its income on food and fuel notices price rises at once, because it cannot easily cut back on either. A wealthier family may barely notice, as a smaller share of its income goes on necessities. Savers are also affected. If a bank pays four per cent a year and prices rise by seven per cent, the money in the account buys less each year, even though the balance is growing. Borrowers can sometimes gain, since the sum they repay is worth less than the sum they received. Economists therefore do not treat inflation as simply good or bad. A slow, steady rise lets businesses and households plan ahead. Rapid and unpredictable rises make planning difficult, because nobody knows what a contract signed today will be worth next year. It is this uncertainty, more than the rise itself, that most worries policymakers.

rc-s005.x: Mangrove trees grow where few other trees can: in salty mud that is flooded twice a day by the tide. Their roots rise above the surface and form a dense tangle, which slows moving water and lets fine mud settle. Over many years this process can build up new land. The tangle of roots also shelters young fish, crabs and prawns, so fishing communities near mangroves often depend on them without realising it. In addition, a wide belt of mangroves can weaken waves during storms, protecting villages behind it. Despite these benefits, mangroves have often been cut for fuel or cleared to make way for shrimp ponds and building plots. Replanting is possible, but it works best when the right species are placed at the right height in the tide, and many early projects failed because the seedlings were planted too low and drowned. Success usually needs the cooperation of local people, who understand the shore better than any visiting planner.

rc-s006.x: A decade ago, many families in small towns had to travel to a bank branch to send money to relatives. The journey cost time and fare, and the queue could be long. Mobile payment services have changed this routine. A shopkeeper now acts as an agent who takes cash and sends a message to the recipient, who collects the amount at another agent nearby or keeps it in a phone account. For households that never had a bank account, this has been a first step into the financial system. The services have their own risks, however. Fraudsters send false messages claiming that money was sent by mistake and ask for it back. Users who share their secret number with a stranger can lose their balance in minutes. Agents may also run out of cash on busy days. Companies and regulators therefore spend considerable effort on teaching users simple habits: never reveal the secret number, check the amount before confirming, and keep receipts. Convenience, it seems, works best when users are careful.

rc-s007.t: The beauty of the written word
rc-s007.x: Calligraphy is the art of making writing beautiful, and it has long been honoured in the Muslim world, partly because it joined two things people valued: the written word and visual design. A calligrapher spends years learning how to cut a reed pen, mix ink and form each letter with the correct proportions. Even a short line may be written many times before it satisfies the artist. Different scripts developed for different uses. Some are upright and clear, suited to copying long texts; others are flowing and decorative, used for titles and for panels on buildings. Learning the rules does not mean copying without thought. Great calligraphers are remembered because they combined strict training with a personal sense of rhythm, so that the same letters look unmistakably theirs. Today computers can produce neat lettering in seconds, yet handwritten calligraphy continues to attract students. Many say that the slow, steady practice teaches patience, and that no machine can reproduce the small variations that give a hand-written page its warmth.

rc-s008.x: Students who stay up all night before an examination believe they are using their time well, yet studies of sleep suggest otherwise. During sleep, the brain does not simply switch off. It appears to replay the events of the day and to strengthen the links that matter, which helps new facts to become lasting memories. People who learn a list of words and then sleep generally recall more of it the next day than people who learn it and stay awake for the same number of hours. Sleep also affects attention. A tired person makes more careless errors and finds it harder to follow a long argument. None of this means that revision is worthless. Facts must be learned before they can be stored. The sensible approach is to study in shorter periods over several days and keep a regular bedtime. A student who does so arrives at the examination with knowledge that has had time to settle, and with a mind able to use it.

rc-s009.x: Before the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand, and a single volume could take months to finish. Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg, working in Mainz, combined movable metal type with a press and an oil-based ink, and printing in Europe changed quickly. A printer could now produce hundreds of identical pages from letters that were arranged, used and then rearranged. Books became cheaper, and more people had reason to learn to read. Printing did not create new ideas by itself, but it allowed them to spread faster than before. A pamphlet written in one city could be reprinted in another within weeks. Authorities sometimes tried to control what was printed, which shows that they understood its power. Historians still debate how large the effect was in each country, because literacy grew slowly and unevenly. What is not in doubt is that texts were no longer rare objects kept in a few libraries. Knowledge had begun to travel in a form that many people could own.

rc-s010.x: City planners often argue about whether new cycle lanes are worth their cost. Critics point out that few commuters cycle in cities where roads are crowded and unsafe, and conclude that lanes would go unused. Supporters reply that the lack of cyclists is the result of danger, not of unwillingness. When a protected lane is built, they say, people who never considered a bicycle begin to try it. Evidence from a number of cities shows that the number of cyclists often rises after a lane opens, although the rise depends on whether the lane links useful places. A lane that stops abruptly at a busy junction is little better than none. Cycling also has benefits that are not obvious from traffic counts. A bicycle takes up little road space, produces no fumes and costs a fraction of a car to run. It follows that even a modest shift from cars may ease congestion and household budgets alike. The real question is not whether lanes cost money but whether they are built where they will be used.

rc-s011.x: Imagine two villages, one beside a river and one among hills. People in the first village can catch fish easily but find it hard to raise sheep, while those in the hills can do the opposite. If each village tries to produce everything for itself, both spend long hours on tasks they do badly. If instead each concentrates on what it does best and trades the surplus, both can have more fish and more wool than before. This idea, called specialisation, lies behind much of the world's trade. It does not require one village to be better at everything; even a village that is slower at both tasks gains by concentrating on the one at which it is less poor. The arrangement is not free of risk, however. A village that depends on a single product suffers if its price falls or if the buyers stop coming. For this reason, successful traders usually specialise while keeping a few other skills in reserve. The lesson of the two villages is that exchange can make both sides better off.

rc-s012.x: In many dry regions, rain arrives in a few heavy showers and then vanishes, running off roofs and roads before anyone can use it. Rainwater harvesting is a simple response: gutters lead the water from a roof into a tank or into a pit where it can soak into the ground. A household with a modest roof can collect many thousands of litres during a single wet season, enough to wash clothes and water a garden for months. Such water is not always safe to drink without treatment, because dust and bird droppings wash down with it, but it is suitable for many other tasks, which reduces pressure on the mains supply. Cities that require new buildings to include a tank have found that the burden on drains during storms also falls. The method is no cure for a serious drought, since a tank cannot fill when no rain falls. Its value lies in making the best use of the rain that does come, and in encouraging people to think of water as a resource to be saved rather than simply spent.

rc-s013.x: Solar panels produce electricity only when the sun shines, but people want to use power at night as well. The usual solution is a battery, which stores energy during the day and releases it later. Batteries have improved greatly, yet they remain expensive and heavy for their size, and they lose capacity slowly as they age. A household that buys one must weigh these costs against the convenience. Some engineers favour other ways to store energy, such as pumping water up to a high tank by day and letting it run down through a turbine at night. This works well where there are hills and spare water, but not on a flat plain. Others point out that energy can be saved simply by using machines when the sun is out, running a water pump at noon rather than at dusk. No single method suits every place. The best plan usually mixes several, chosen according to local conditions, cost and the habits of those who will use the power.

rc-s014.x: For centuries, many village songs were never written down. They passed from one singer to the next, usually learned in childhood at weddings and harvest gatherings. Because each singer remembered the song a little differently, versions of the same tune could vary from valley to valley. This was not carelessness. Singers changed words to suit the occasion, added a verse about a local event or dropped one that no longer made sense, and so the song stayed alive. When collectors began to record such songs on tape, they faced a difficult choice. A recording preserves one performance exactly, but it can make the song seem fixed, as if that single version were the correct one. Some collectors therefore recorded the same song from several singers and kept all the versions. Others worry that people may begin to copy the recording instead of singing from memory, and that the habit of change will fade. The question is not whether to record, since lost songs cannot be recovered, but how to record without freezing a living tradition.

rc-s015.x: Antibiotics are drugs that kill bacteria or stop them from multiplying. They do not work against viruses, so they are no use for a common cold. Bacteria in a large population are not all identical, and a few may by chance be able to survive a particular drug. If the drug is used often, the weaker bacteria die and the tougher ones multiply in their place, so that the next infection may be harder to treat. This is how resistance arises. It is made worse when people take antibiotics for illnesses they cannot cure, or use them without a doctor's advice. Doctors now try to prescribe antibiotics only when they are needed and to explain how they should be taken. Scientists are also searching for new drugs, but the process takes years. In the meantime the most practical defence is careful use: antibiotics are a limited resource, and every unnecessary dose makes the drugs a little less reliable for the person who truly needs them.

rc-s016.t: The road of silk and more
rc-s016.x: The name 'Silk Road' suggests a single highway, but it was in fact a network of routes crossing deserts, mountains and plains between China and lands to the west. Few merchants travelled the whole distance. Goods were passed from trader to trader, each of whom sold at a profit to the next, so a bale of silk might change hands many times before it reached its final buyer. Silk was only one of the goods carried. Spices, paper, glass, horses and metalwork also moved along the routes, as did ideas, religious beliefs and crafts. Cities that sat at the meeting points of routes, such as Samarkand and Kashgar, grew rich as markets and as places to rest. Travel was slow and often dangerous, and caravans paid fees to rulers whose lands they crossed. Historians use the term cautiously now, because it can hide how varied the trade was. Even so, the picture of goods and ideas passing along linked routes remains a useful way to understand how distant peoples influenced one another.

rc-s017.x: Many charities rely on volunteers, and the usual view is that volunteers help others at their own cost. That is true, but it is only half of the picture. People who give their time regularly often report that they gain something in return. A retired clerk who teaches arithmetic to children after school may find that he feels useful again. A student who helps in a hospital reception may learn how to speak calmly to frightened people, a skill that no classroom lesson quite teaches. Volunteering also brings together people who would not otherwise meet, from different ages and backgrounds, and so builds the sort of trust that makes a neighbourhood function. None of this should be used as an excuse to treat volunteers as free labour. Organisations that value them train them, give them clear tasks and thank them sincerely. When a volunteer is left without guidance, the experience can be frustrating for everyone. Giving time works best when it is a fair exchange of effort and respect on both sides.

rc-s018.x: On a hot afternoon, the temperature on a paved street in a city can be several degrees higher than in a nearby park. Concrete and asphalt soak up sunlight during the day and give the heat back slowly after dark, so that crowded districts stay warm long into the night. Trees reduce this effect in two ways. Their leaves cast shade, which keeps the ground cooler, and they release water vapour, which cools the air much as sweat cools skin. A row of mature trees along a road can make walking pleasant when the open street beyond is uncomfortable. Planting is not as simple as it sounds, however. Young trees need regular watering for several years, and the wrong species can damage pavements with their roots or drop heavy branches in storms. Councils that succeed usually choose local species suited to the soil and climate, and involve residents in looking after the saplings. The benefits, such as lower cooling costs and cleaner, more attractive streets, arrive slowly, but they last for decades.

rc-s019.x: Every wave of automation has produced the same fear: that machines will take work and leave people with nothing to do. History offers a mixed answer. When mechanical looms spread in the nineteenth century, many hand weavers lost their livelihoods, and the hardship was real. Yet cloth became cheaper, demand for it grew, and new jobs appeared in repairing machines, selling cloth and building factories. The overall number of jobs did not fall, although the jobs were different and not always offered to the same people. This is the point that careful observers stress. The question is not only whether work will exist but whether workers can move into it. A weaver of fifty cannot easily become a machine engineer. Training, savings to live on during a change, and support for those who must move can decide whether automation brings widespread benefit or widespread distress. Today's discussions about computers and robots echo the old ones. The lesson from the past is neither to welcome every machine without thought nor to resist all of them, but to prepare people for the change.

rc-s020.x: In many Pakistani neighbourhoods, a group of ten neighbours agrees to put the same sum into a common pot each month. Each month one member takes the whole pot, and the order is fixed at the start, often by drawing lots. After ten months every member has paid in ten times and received the pot once. No interest is paid, and there is no bank. The arrangement works because the members trust one another, and because each knows that a member who failed to pay would lose the respect of the group. For a family that finds it hard to save a large sum alone, the system acts as a discipline. The money has already left the house before it can be spent on something else, and the pot arrives as a lump sum that can pay for a wedding, a machine or school fees. Its weakness is that the member who takes the pot last has lent to the others for months without reward, and a defaulter can damage the whole circle. Careful groups therefore choose their members with care.

rc-x001.t: Why the sea rises and falls
rc-x001.x: The regular rise and fall of the sea, known as the tide, is caused mainly by the pull of the Moon's gravity on the water of the Earth. The side of the Earth facing the Moon is pulled towards it, and the water there bulges outwards. Another bulge forms on the far side, so most coasts experience two high tides and two low tides in a little over a day. The Sun also pulls on the oceans, but because it is so much farther away its effect is smaller than the Moon's. When the Sun and Moon are lined up with the Earth, their pulls combine, and the tides are at their highest and lowest. When they are at right angles to each other, the tides are less extreme. The shape of the coast also matters. In a narrow bay the water is squeezed, and the tide can rise much higher than in the open sea. Sailors and fishermen have long relied on tide tables to plan their work, because arriving at a harbour at the wrong hour can leave a boat stranded on the mud.

rc-x002.x: Some people say they have no time to read, yet many of them spend an hour each day looking at a phone. The difference is less about time than about habit. A person who begins with ten pages a day will finish a book in a month or so, and the habit soon grows. The key is to choose something enjoyable rather than something that merely seems impressive. A reader who forces himself through a dull book often gives up reading altogether, while a lively story or an interesting account of a subject he cares about keeps him turning pages. Reading also trains attention in a way that short videos do not, because it asks the mind to follow an idea through many sentences. Over time this builds vocabulary and the ability to express thoughts clearly. It is not necessary to finish every book. Putting a book aside when it fails to interest you is a sensible choice, not a failure. What matters is that reading becomes a regular and pleasant part of the day.

rc-x003.x: Before telephones, the post was the way ordinary people kept in touch across distance, and a good postal system was one of the most valuable services a government could provide. The idea of a fixed charge for a letter, paid in advance by the sender with a stamp, was introduced in Britain in 1840 and soon copied elsewhere. Earlier, the receiver often paid on delivery, and many refused letters they could not afford. The prepaid stamp made posting simpler and faster, and the number of letters grew rapidly. Railways then carried mail over long distances far more quickly than coaches, and sorting could be done on the train itself. In places such as the Indian subcontinent, the post office reached remote villages and became a trusted public institution. People used it not only for letters but also to send money and to save small sums. Today messages travel in seconds, and few people write letters, yet the post still carries parcels and documents. Its history shows how a simple change, such as the stamp, can alter the habits of a whole society.

questions.s: The ______ of the desert makes it hard for plants to survive there.
questions.e: Plants struggle in a desert because it is extremely dry, which is aridity. Fertility, humidity and abundance would all help plants grow, so they contradict the sentence.

questions.s: The hospital staff worked ______ to save the injured passengers after the bus accident.
questions.e: Saving lives after an accident calls for constant effort: tirelessly. The other adverbs describe poor work.

questions.s: The teacher's ______ explanation helped even the weakest students understand the lesson at once.
questions.e: The explanation helped weak students understand immediately, so it must have been clear: lucid. A vague explanation would have confused them, and length or haste does not guarantee understanding.

questions.s: Zara is both clever and ______; she always shares her notes with classmates.
questions.e: Sharing notes shows generosity. Selfish, miserly and secretive people would keep them.

questions.s: The soldiers showed great ______ by defending the border despite being outnumbered.
questions.e: Defending a border against greater numbers requires bravery. Cowardice is the opposite.

questions.s: The explorer was ______ in the face of danger, but ______ when he returned to the quiet routine of ordinary life.
questions.e: A man bold in danger who gets restless in quiet life is intrepid ... restless. A timid explorer would not suit the contrast, and cautious ... fearless reverses it.

questions.s: Faisal's ______ spending left him without savings, even though his salary was above average.
questions.e: Having no savings despite a good salary shows wasteful spending: profligate. Prudent, thrifty and modest spending would leave savings.

questions.s: The festival was a ______ occasion, filled with laughter and noise, in sharp contrast to the ______ mood of the preceding week.
questions.e: "In sharp contrast" demands opposite moods: laughter and noise is festive, so the previous week was sombre. The reversed pair contradicts the laughter, and the other pairs give similar rather than contrasting moods.

questions.s: Because the road was ______ with ice, drivers moved very slowly and carefully.
questions.e: Ice makes a surface slippery, which explains the slow, careful driving. A crowded or narrow road might slow traffic, but the sentence names ice as the cause.

questions.s: Mahnoor spoke with such ______ that no one doubted she was telling the truth.
questions.e: Belief in her words comes from sincerity. Insolence, confusion and hesitation would raise doubt.

questions.s: The vendor's cart was ______ with fruit, so that nothing more could be added.
questions.e: Nothing more could be added means it was full: laden. Bare, lacking and stripped mean empty.

questions.s: The minister's resignation was ______, coming as it did without any warning, and the party was left in ______.
questions.e: Sudden resignation without warning leaves a party in confusion: abrupt ... disarray. Expected or gradual resignation would not disturb the party.

questions.s: The treasurer ______ the funds so carefully that not a single rupee was wasted.
questions.e: Not wasting a rupee means managing carefully: husbanded. Squandered, misplaced and neglected imply waste or loss.

questions.s: Many of the customs of the region have become ______ in the modern world, yet a few old men still ______ them faithfully.
questions.e: "Yet" shows contrast between customs that are out of date and a few men who keep following them: obsolete ... observe. The other pairs break the contrast logic.

questions.s: The council's decision to close the library was ______ by the residents, who signed petitions and held a protest.
questions.e: Petitions and protests show strong opposition. Welcomed, accepted and praised all indicate approval or calm, which contradicts the action taken.

questions.s: The company's spokesman made a ______ statement that avoided answering any of the journalists' direct questions.
questions.e: Avoiding direct questions means saying nothing of substance: bland, or evasive. Candid, forthright and detailed statements would answer them.

questions.s: Although the shopkeeper was known for being ______, he surprised everyone by giving the poor family a generous discount.
questions.e: The word "Although" signals a contrast with the generous act, so the shopkeeper's known trait must be the opposite: stingy. "Generous" would remove the contrast and make the sentence illogical.

questions.s: The thief moved ______ through the dark house so that no one would hear him.
questions.e: Not wanting to be heard means moving quietly and secretly: stealthily. Noisily is the opposite, and cheerfully or lazily say nothing about avoiding detection.

questions.s: Farhan was a ______ speaker whose voice rose and fell so skilfully that no one noticed the time passing.
questions.e: Listeners not noticing time shows an engaging speaker: captivating. Monotonous and dreary would make time drag.

questions.s: He was ______ of his friend's success and secretly wished that he had won the award himself.
questions.e: Secretly wishing for his friend's award is envy. A proud person would be glad for the friend, and the other words do not explain the wish.

questions.s: It rained so ______ that the streets of the city were flooded within an hour.
questions.e: Flooding within an hour requires very heavy rain. Lightly and gently would not flood streets, and "rarely" does not suit the grammar.

questions.s: The residents were ______ to the noise of the railway and no longer noticed the trains passing.
questions.e: Not noticing trains anymore results from getting used to them: accustomed. Hostile, alert or sensitive residents would notice them.

questions.s: The new rules were ______ by the staff, who found them so vague that no two people could agree on what they ______.
questions.e: Vague rules leave staff unable to agree on what is required, so they are criticised. "Welcomed" or "praised" does not fit "so vague", and vague rules would not be memorised.

questions.s: Hira found her colleague's constant ______ more irritating than any open quarrel, since it was never ______ directly.
questions.e: Sarcasm that is never openly stated, so cannot be addressed, fits "irritating". Honesty or praise would not irritate in that way.

questions.s: Though poor, the family was ______ and never took anything that was not theirs.
questions.e: "Though poor" is followed by a virtue: honest, since they never took what was not theirs. Wealthy contradicts "poor".

questions.s: The goalkeeper's ______ save in the final minute secured the title for the team.
questions.e: A save that wins a title is outstanding: spectacular. Trivial, clumsy and routine would not be described as securing a title.

questions.s: A ______ glance at the headlines was all he had time for before leaving for work.
questions.e: Only a short glance means a quick, superficial look: cursory. Thorough, careful and detailed need more time.

questions.s: The ______ test questions were so easy that everyone finished in half the time.
questions.e: Finishing in half the time points to easy questions: simple. Obscure, confusing and lengthy questions would take longer.

questions.s: The scholarship was awarded not on wealth but on ______, so even the poorest students could compete.
questions.e: Even poor students could compete, which suggests ability as the basis: merit. Inheritance and influence would favour the rich.

questions.s: The ______ of the old regime was so complete that within a year hardly anyone remembered its leaders.
questions.e: Being forgotten within a year points to total erasure: obliteration. Persistence, restoration and glorification would keep the leaders in memory.

questions.s: The ______ road through the hills had so many sharp turns that she felt dizzy.
questions.e: Many sharp turns describe a winding road. Straight, level and smooth roads have no such turns.

questions.s: The wolf is ______ by nature, avoiding human settlements wherever it can.
questions.e: Avoiding people means being difficult to find or meet: elusive. Sociable, domestic and friendly describe the opposite.

questions.s: The ______ of the sun made it impossible to look at the sky without squinting.
questions.e: Squinting is a response to harsh bright light: glare. Shade and a setting sun would be easier on the eyes, and warmth does not cause squinting.

questions.s: The architect's design was ______, its clean lines and absence of decoration reflecting a philosophy that valued function over show.
questions.e: Clean lines and absence of decoration describe austere design. Baroque, opulent and ornate all mean richly decorated.

questions.s: Instead of ______ the quarrel, the mediator's clumsy remarks only ______ it.
questions.e: "Instead of" and "only" show the mediator failed in the intended task: she meant to resolve the quarrel but inflamed it. The reversed pair makes the mediator's intention nonsensical, and the other pairs imply success.

questions.s: A good leader must be ______ enough to listen to the opinions of others.
questions.e: Listening to others requires humility. Arrogant and stubborn leaders refuse to listen, and hasty ones do not wait.

questions.s: It would be ______ to expect a beginner to master the language in a month; such a goal is ______ at best.
questions.e: Expecting mastery in a month is unrealistic, and "at best" fits ambitious. The other pairs praise the goal.

questions.s: The scientist was ______ to explain the anomaly, since every attempt to fit it into the accepted theory only ______ the problem.
questions.e: Failed attempts that only worsen the problem leave her unable; "compounded" means made worse. Resolved or settled would mean success.

questions.s: The teacher asked the students to remain ______ while the guest was speaking.
questions.e: Listening to a guest requires attention: attentive. Restless and noisy contradict the request, and absent cannot describe students who remain.

questions.s: Her ______ attitude towards the project, neither supporting nor opposing it, frustrated colleagues who wanted a firm decision.
questions.e: Neither supporting nor opposing is a noncommittal, uncertain stance: equivocal. Zealous, vehement and resolute all describe firm commitment and would not frustrate people wanting a decision.

questions.s: Though the plan was ______ in theory, its practical difficulties were so ______ that it was never put into effect.
questions.e: "Though" shows contrast: sound in theory, but formidable obstacles prevented it. Minor or negligible difficulties would not stop the plan.

questions.s: Asif's ______ remark at the funeral shocked the mourners, who felt it showed no respect for the dead.
questions.e: A remark that seems disrespectful in a solemn setting is flippant. Solemn, sincere and poignant remarks would respect the occasion.

questions.s: The newspaper's report was ______, giving only the facts and avoiding any ______ of opinion.
questions.e: Giving only facts and avoiding opinion is objective; "hint" completes "avoiding any hint of opinion". A biased report would carry opinion, so it could not avoid it.

questions.s: Instead of settling the dispute, the new law only ______ it, since both parties now claimed it supported them.
questions.e: "Instead of" and "only" show the law made things worse: aggravated. Resolved, settled and ended would mean success.

questions.s: The shopkeeper's honesty was ______; customers had never known him to cheat anyone.
questions.e: Never cheating anyone means his honesty is beyond doubt. Dubious, doubtful and suspect are contradicted.

questions.s: The company's profits ______ sharply during the recession, forcing it to dismiss many workers.
questions.e: Dismissing workers suggests money problems, so profits fell steeply: plummeted. Soared and multiplied describe increases, which would not force job cuts.

questions.s: The scientist's ______ approach, checking every result three times, made her findings very reliable.
questions.e: Checking every result three times is careful and thorough, which is what meticulous means. The other words describe the opposite attitude and would not make findings reliable.

questions.s: The athlete trained ______ every morning, never missing a single session.
questions.e: Never missing a session means training regularly. Rarely and seldom contradict it.

questions.s: The treasurer kept an ______ record of expenses, so every rupee spent could be traced to a receipt.
questions.e: Tracing every rupee to a receipt requires a correct, complete record: accurate. Incomplete, imaginary and arbitrary records could not be traced.

questions.s: The cricket match was ______ because of heavy rain, and the players went home.
questions.e: Players going home in heavy rain means play stopped: abandoned. Won, enjoyed and televised do not explain leaving.

questions.s: The medicine is ______ in small doses but can be dangerous if taken in excess.
questions.e: The contrast with "dangerous if taken in excess" shows that small doses help: beneficial. Fatal or useless small doses would not need the contrast.

questions.s: Because the library was ______, students could study without any disturbance.
questions.e: Studying without disturbance requires quiet. A noisy or crowded library would disturb, and a locked one could not be used.

questions.s: Bilal was so ______ after the long march that he fell asleep as soon as he reached home.
questions.e: Falling asleep at once after a long march points to extreme tiredness. Anxious or curious people tend to stay awake, and a cheerful mood does not explain instant sleep.

questions.s: The speaker's argument was ______ by emotion rather than evidence; it carried the crowd but would not have survived a ______ examination.
questions.e: An argument relying on emotion carries a crowd but fails careful scrutiny: driven by emotion, and rigorous examination would defeat it. The other pairs make evidence or examination irrelevant.

questions.s: The sudden drop in temperature ______ the growth of the seedlings, which stayed small for weeks.
questions.e: Seedlings that stay small were held back: stunted. Hastened, nourished and supported would produce faster or stronger growth.

questions.s: The river was ______ after the monsoon, covering the fields on both banks.
questions.e: Water covering the fields means the river had risen: swollen. Shallow and dry rivers would not flood, and frozen does not cause covering.

questions.s: Bilal is a ______ student who completes every assignment before the due date.
questions.e: Completing every task early shows hard work: diligent. The other adjectives suggest neglect.

questions.s: Rafia was ______ about the interview, so she practised her answers every evening for a week.
questions.e: Practising every evening suggests worry about doing well: anxious. Careless, indifferent or bored people would not prepare so hard.

questions.s: Her ______ remarks about her colleagues' work made her unpopular, though she insisted she was only being honest.
questions.e: Remarks that make a person unpopular while she claims honesty are harsh and biting: caustic. Flattering and diplomatic remarks would make her liked, and tentative remarks would not cause offence.

questions.s: The prime exhibit was kept in a ______ glass case to protect it from thieves and dust.
questions.e: Protecting from thieves and dust requires a closed case: sealed. Cracked or open would not protect.

questions.s: Because the committee had been ______ in its work, the report was ready a month before the deadline.
questions.e: Finishing early shows hard, careful work: diligent. Negligent, dilatory and lax all describe slackness and would cause delay.

questions.s: The minister gave a ______ reply; he neither accepted nor rejected the demand.
questions.e: Neither accepting nor rejecting is noncommittal. Decisive, emphatic and categorical replies take a firm position.

questions.s: The two articles were so alike that the editor suspected one had been ______ from the other.
questions.e: Extremely close similarity suggests copying: plagiarised. The other verbs would not raise suspicion by themselves.

questions.s: The new policy was intended to ______ the burden on farmers, not to add to their troubles.
questions.e: "Not to add to their troubles" shows the policy aims to reduce the burden: alleviate. Aggravate means to worsen, which is the reverse of the intention.

questions.s: Having lost his way in the mountains, the traveller was grateful for the ______ shown by the villagers.
questions.e: Being grateful implies kind treatment: hospitality. Hostility, indifference and suspicion would not make a lost traveller grateful.

questions.s: Wasting water is ______ because clean water is limited in many parts of the country.
questions.e: If clean water is scarce, wasting it is irresponsible. Calling it admirable, harmless or sensible would contradict the reason given.

questions.s: The patient was too ______ to walk, so the nurse brought him a wheelchair.
questions.e: Needing a wheelchair shows that he lacks strength. A strong or eager patient could walk.

questions.s: The inventor's early failures, far from ______ him, only ______ his resolve to try again.
questions.e: "Far from" and "only" mean the failures did not discourage him and in fact strengthened his resolve. Pairs such as "encouraging ... weakened" put the two halves in the wrong relation.

questions.s: The author's later novels ______ the promise of her first book; critics found them dull and predictable.
questions.e: Dull, predictable novels did not live up to early promise. Exceeded or confirmed would mean the later books were good, which the critics deny.

questions.s: The charity's appeal was so ______ that donations, which had been ______ for months, doubled within a week.
questions.e: Doubling after months of no growth reflects a powerful appeal and previously stagnant giving. Bland or tedious appeals would not double donations.

questions.s: The bridge was too ______ to bear the weight of heavy trucks, so only cars were allowed.
questions.e: Only cars being allowed shows the bridge was weak: fragile. A massive bridge could carry trucks.

questions.s: The mosque's dome, ______ by the afternoon sun, could be seen from miles away.
questions.e: Visibility from far away goes with being lit by the sun: illuminated. Concealed, darkened and shaded would hide it.

questions.s: It was ______ that a boy who had never travelled alone would reach the city safely, yet he arrived without any trouble.
questions.e: "Yet" introduces the surprise; before it, success seemed unlikely: improbable. Certain, expected or natural would not need "yet".

questions.s: The professor's ______ of the theory was so thorough that no student had any question left.
questions.e: Having no questions left follows from a full explanation: exposition. Rejection, omission and concealment would leave questions.

questions.s: The treaty was ______ by a minor clause that each side interpreted differently, and so the peace it established proved ______.
questions.e: A clause open to different readings weakens the agreement, so the peace is fragile. Pairs showing strength or stability contradict the disagreement.

questions.s: The judge remained ______ throughout the trial, favouring neither the plaintiff nor the defendant.
questions.e: Favouring neither side is the definition of impartial. A biased judge would favour one party, and silence or fury says nothing about fairness.

questions.s: She felt a ______ pride in her village's school, although she had left it long ago and owed it no ______.
questions.e: Pride that remains after leaving, despite no duty owed, is lingering; "obligation" completes the sense of no duty. The other pairs do not combine meaningfully.

questions.s: The ______ of the evidence left the jury in no doubt that the accused was guilty.
questions.e: No doubt in the jury follows from strong evidence, hence its weight. Absence or flimsiness would produce doubt.

questions.s: The explorer's account was full of ______ details, but later investigators found that many of them were invented.
questions.e: "But" signals a contrast: the details seemed believable until they were found to be invented, so convincing fits. Boring or brief details would not need to be disproved.

questions.s: The shirt was so ______ that she washed it three times, but the stain did not fade.
questions.e: A stain that does not fade after three washes means the shirt was badly dirty: soiled. A spotless shirt would not need washing.

questions.s: The treaty was meant to ______ peace, but its unfair terms only ______ the resentment between the two nations.
questions.e: "Meant to" shows the aim was to secure peace, and "only" introduces the unintended result: unfair terms deepened resentment. Removing resentment would mean the treaty worked, and destroying peace was not its aim.

questions.s: The report was ______ in its criticism, naming every department that had failed to meet the deadline.
questions.e: Naming every failing department leaves no one spared: unsparing. Lenient or apologetic reports would soften the criticism, and ambiguous ones would not name names.

questions.s: While the first proposal was ______, the second was so detailed that it was approved without changes.
questions.e: "While" contrasts the first with the very detailed second: sketchy. Thorough, precise and elaborate would match the second rather than contrast.

questions.s: Although Nida seemed calm on the surface, she was inwardly ______ about the results.
questions.e: "Although" contrasts outward calm with inner worry: agitated. Serene, contented and confident would match the calm.

questions.s: Students who ______ their time well usually find that they can revise every subject before the exams.
questions.e: Finishing revision comes from using time wisely: manage. Squander, waste and lose would leave too little time.

questions.s: The poet's verse, once ______ by critics as old-fashioned, is now ______ as a masterpiece of its age.
questions.e: "Once... now" sets a changed judgement: first dismissed as old-fashioned, then celebrated as a masterpiece. The other pairs either reverse this or fail to show a reversal.

questions.s: The architect's plan was ______ with the budget, since the cost of materials was far greater than the sum available.
questions.e: Cost far above funds shows the plan could not fit the budget: incompatible. Consistent and identical mean the opposite.

questions.s: The company rewarded its employees' ______ with an annual bonus.
questions.e: Bonuses reward faithful service: loyalty. The others are not rewarded.

questions.s: The ______ rise of the river after the storm forced villagers to leave their homes within hours.
questions.e: Having to leave within hours implies a rapid rise: sudden. Gradual, gentle and slow would allow more time.

questions.s: The two witnesses gave ______ accounts of the accident, so the police could not tell which of them was telling the truth.
questions.e: Police cannot decide whom to believe when the accounts disagree: contradictory. Identical or supportive accounts would settle the matter.

questions.s: His ______ speech, full of unnecessary words, took twenty minutes to say what could have been said in two.
questions.e: Taking twenty minutes for a two-minute message means wordiness: prolix. Pithy, succinct and concise mean brief.

questions.s: The villagers ______ the stranger with suspicion because outsiders rarely visited their remote valley.
questions.e: Suspicion towards a rare outsider shows how they regarded him. Honoured, envied or obeyed do not go with suspicion.

questions.s: Sana speaks so ______ that people in the last row can barely hear her.
questions.e: People in the back barely hearing her means she speaks quietly. Loudly and clearly would help them hear.

questions.s: Though the committee's decision seemed ______ at first, its reasons became clear once the full facts were published.
questions.e: "Though... at first" and "reasons became clear" show it looked random and unreasoned before: arbitrary. Justified or calculated would already have appeared sensible.

questions.s: Far from being ______, the committee's report was a detailed and balanced study of the problem.
questions.e: "Far from" introduces the opposite of "detailed and balanced"; a shallow report is superficial. Exhaustive and impartial would agree with the description rather than contrast with it.

questions.s: His ______ lie was quickly discovered, since the facts did not match his story.
questions.e: A lie found out quickly was badly made: clumsy. A clever lie would not be discovered so easily.

questions.s: Everyone applauded the ______ performance of the young gymnast.
questions.e: Applause follows an excellent performance: flawless. Clumsy, dull and poor performances do not earn applause.

questions.s: The senator's speech was a ______ of clichés, every sentence ______ with phrases the audience had heard a hundred times.
questions.e: A speech that reuses familiar phrases is a medley of clichés crowded with stock phrases. Free or fresh would mean no clichés.

questions.s: The ______ rise in fuel prices left many families unable to afford daily travel.
questions.e: Families being unable to afford travel needs a sharp increase: steep. Gradual, negligible and slight would not cause such trouble.

questions.s: Because the food was ______ prepared, many guests fell ill after the wedding dinner.
questions.e: Illness after a meal suggests bad preparation: poorly. Lovingly, expertly and lavishly suggest a good meal.

questions.s: He made a ______ attempt to hide his disappointment, but his face gave him away.
questions.e: His face betrayed him, so the attempt was weak: feeble. Successful, skilful and convincing would have hidden it.

questions.s: Though the soup was ______, Ali ate it politely rather than offend his hostess.
questions.e: "Though... rather than offend" shows that eating was a courtesy despite poor taste: unpalatable. Delicious, nourishing and fragrant would need no politeness.

questions.s: The soldiers were rewarded for their ______ in defending the post against heavy attack.
questions.e: Rewards go to bravery: valour. Timidity, laziness and folly are not rewarded.

questions.s: To the surprise of the team, the experiment ______ their hypothesis; the results were exactly the opposite of what they predicted.
questions.e: Results opposite to the prediction disprove the hypothesis: refuted. Confirmed and supported would mean the results matched.

questions.s: The two friends settled the matter ______, without any shouting or quarrel.
questions.e: Without shouting or quarrel means in a friendly manner: amicably. Bitterly, angrily and violently suggest conflict.

questions.s: The decision to build the dam was ______ because it would displace thousands of villagers even as it provided electricity.
questions.e: A choice with both benefits and harms is disputed: controversial. Unanimous or welcome would imply broad agreement, and trivial minimises serious effects.

questions.s: The new manager was ______ in his approach, introducing changes slowly and consulting everyone first.
questions.e: Slow changes with consultation are careful: cautious. Reckless, impulsive and hasty would imply sudden change.

questions.s: The thick fog ______ the view so badly that the pilot postponed the flight.
questions.e: Postponing a flight because of fog means the view was blocked: obscured. Improved would not lead to a delay.

questions.s: The singer's voice was so ______ that the entire hall fell silent to listen.
questions.e: A whole hall falling silent shows a captivating voice: enchanting. Harsh or ordinary voices would not do it, and a faint one would not be heard by all.

questions.s: The speaker was ______ to the criticism, replying politely and without any sign of anger.
questions.e: Replying politely shows openness to criticism: receptive. Hostile and deaf do not fit, and immune would not explain the polite reply.

questions.s: Imran's ______ habit of arriving late made his teammates stop relying on him.
questions.e: Teammates stopping reliance follows from lateness that happens repeatedly: chronic. Occasional, rare or accidental lateness would not destroy trust.

questions.s: The company's growth was ______, rising year after year without a single setback, while its competitors rose and fell ______.
questions.e: Uninterrupted yearly growth is steady, in contrast to competitors who rose and fell erratically. The reversed pair mixes the two.

questions.s: The old well had been ______ for years, so the villagers now fetch water from the canal.
questions.e: Fetching water elsewhere shows the well is no longer used: abandoned. Restored, deepened or cherished would keep it in use.

questions.s: The more the lawyer ______ the witness, the more contradictory the testimony became.
questions.e: Testimony becoming contradictory under pressure comes from repeated questioning. Thanking, ignoring or praising would not expose contradictions.

questions.s: The shopkeeper's prices were ______ enough to attract customers from distant towns.
questions.e: Attracting distant customers needs low or fair prices: reasonable. Exorbitant, inflated and prohibitive would drive them away.

questions.s: Not wishing to ______ her guests by keeping them waiting, Mrs Siddiqui served the meal on time.
questions.e: Keeping guests waiting would upset them, so she acted to avoid that: offend. Impress, invite and entertain are all things a host wants to do, so "not wishing to" does not fit them.

questions.s: The government's ______ to curb corruption won it support from honest citizens.
questions.e: Support follows from a firm commitment: determination. Reluctance, failure and refusal would lose support.

questions.s: The elder brother was ______ and thoughtful, while the younger was impulsive and ______.
questions.e: The conjunction "while" contrasts thoughtful with impulsive, so the pair deliberate ... rash lines up. Hasty ... prudent reverses the order.

questions.s: Although the museum's collection is ______, it contains a few items of great historical value.
questions.e: "Although" sets a small whole against a few valuable items: modest. Vast, renowned or priceless collections would not need the qualification.

questions.s: The critic's praise was so ______ that the author suspected it was meant to flatter him rather than judge his book.
questions.e: Excessive, gushing praise looks like flattery: effusive. Grudging, measured or perfunctory praise would be restrained and would not arouse that suspicion.

questions.s: The director was known for his ______ style: he wasted no words and expected the same from his staff.
questions.e: Wasting no words describes a brief, clipped style: terse. Verbose, florid and rambling are all wordy.

questions.s: The defendant's alibi was so ______ that the prosecutor, though certain of his guilt, could not ______ it.
questions.e: Being unable to challenge it means the alibi was unbreakable: watertight, and he could not dislodge it. A flimsy alibi would be easy to break down.

questions.s: Her ______ wit made even the stern examiners smile, though she never mocked anyone.
questions.e: Wit that makes stern people smile without mocking anyone is charming and defuses tension: disarming. Abrasive and sardonic wit would offend or mock, which the sentence denies.

questions.s: Maryam's ______ handwriting was so clear that the examiner read her paper without any difficulty.
questions.e: Reading without difficulty means the writing could be read easily: legible. Illegible is the opposite, and cramped or ornate writing tends to be harder to read.

questions.s: Khalid ______ his words carefully, knowing that one careless remark could cost him the job.
questions.e: Fear of a careless remark leads to careful consideration: weighed. Wasted or multiplied words would not protect him.

questions.s: Her ______ on the subject was so well known that no one expected her to change her view, however strong the argument.
questions.e: Nobody expecting her to change her view shows stubborn firmness: obduracy. Flexibility and ambivalence mean willingness to change or uncertainty, and diffidence is shyness.

questions.s: A healthy diet is ______ for children, since their bodies are still growing.
questions.e: Growing bodies need good food, so a healthy diet is essential. Calling it optional or harmful contradicts the reason given after "since".

questions.s: The vaccine campaign was ______ successful, reducing the disease by more than ninety per cent within five years.
questions.e: A reduction of over ninety per cent is a striking success: remarkably. Barely, partially and scarcely would suggest small success.

questions.s: The mountaineers were ______ by the sudden storm, which forced them to abandon the climb.
questions.e: A storm forcing them to abandon the climb prevented their plan, which is thwarted. The other verbs describe pleasant outcomes that do not fit abandoning the climb.

questions.s: The festival ______ thousands of visitors to Lahore each spring, filling its hotels and restaurants.
questions.e: Full hotels and restaurants result from visitors being drawn in: attracts. Repels or ignores would empty them.

questions.s: The prisoner showed no ______ for his crime and even boasted about it.
questions.e: Boasting shows he felt no regret: remorse. The others do not fit what boasting would contradict.

questions.s: The principal praised the ______ of the volunteers who had cleaned the park without being asked.
questions.e: Acting without being asked shows initiative. Laziness, neglect and hesitation are not praised.

questions.s: The ______ of the clues made the puzzle hard to solve; each hint seemed to point in a different direction.
questions.e: Hints pointing in different directions are inconsistent. Simplicity and clarity would make solving easy.

questions.s: Not only was the proposal ______, it was also impractical, since no one could afford to carry it out.
questions.e: "Not only... also impractical" adds a second fault; the cost point shows it was extravagant. Modest, sensible and cheap would not be faults.

questions.s: The hikers, ______ by the steep path, stopped at every bend to catch their breath.
questions.e: Stopping to catch breath shows they were out of breath: winded. Refreshed would not need stops, and amused or bored does not explain them.

questions.s: The farmer was delighted because the rains were ______ this year, giving him a bumper wheat crop.
questions.e: A bumper crop and delight show the rains were abundant: plentiful. Scarce rain would reduce the crop and cause worry, which contradicts the sentence.

questions.s: Mansoor accepted the criticism ______, thanking his teacher for pointing out the errors.
questions.e: Thanking the critic shows a gracious acceptance. The other adverbs suggest displeasure.

questions.s: The lawyer's argument was so ______ that the jury had no choice but to agree with it.
questions.e: Jurors who must agree have been convinced by a forceful argument: compelling. A tedious, irrelevant or frivolous argument would not leave them without choice.

questions.s: The children were ______ with excitement on the last day before the holidays.
questions.e: "Bursting with excitement" is the natural phrase. Void, empty and lacking all describe absence of excitement.

questions.s: Hania's reply was so ______ that the interviewer thanked her for being direct.
questions.e: Being thanked for directness shows honesty: candid. Devious and evasive replies would not be thanked.

questions.s: The dictator's rule was ______ and left no room for ______ of any kind.
questions.e: A rule leaving no room for opposition is oppressive, and what it forbids is dissent. Generous or liberal rule would permit protest and criticism, so those pairs contradict "no room".

questions.s: The two neighbours ______ their old quarrel and began to greet each other warmly.
questions.e: Greeting each other warmly shows the quarrel was put aside. Renewed or exaggerated would keep them hostile.

questions.s: The ______ between the two brothers lasted for decades, ending only when their father fell ill.
questions.e: A conflict that lasts decades and ends when a crisis arrives is a feud. Alliance, partnership and agreement all imply cooperation and would not need an illness to end them.

questions.s: Mr Qureshi is very ______, always arriving ten minutes before the appointed time.
questions.e: Always arriving early shows punctuality. The other words describe neglect or absence.

questions.s: Ahmed forgot his umbrella, so he got ______ on the way to school.
questions.e: Without an umbrella in the rain, he would be soaked: drenched. Dusty, bored and hungry do not follow from forgetting an umbrella.

questions.s: Although the exam was ______ for most candidates, Zainab found it ______ and finished early.
questions.e: "Although" marks a contrast, and finishing early shows Zainab found it easy while most found it difficult. The reversed pair contradicts finishing early, and the last two pairs do not set up any contrast.

questions.s: The politician's promises were so ______ that few voters could say what he actually intended to do.
questions.e: If voters cannot say what he intended, the promises were unclear: ambiguous. Specific promises would be easy to understand, so that option contradicts the result.

questions.s: The orchestra's performance was ______; critics could not recall a more moving concert in the city.
questions.e: Critics unable to recall a better concert points to an outstanding one: memorable. Forgettable and mediocre contradict this, and brief says nothing about quality.

questions.s: The ______ of the examination hall was broken only by the scratching of pens.
questions.e: Only pen scratching being heard means the hall was silent. Clamour, laughter and music are noises.

questions.s: The old man was ______ about modern gadgets; he refused to use a mobile phone or a computer.
questions.e: Refusing to use the devices shows doubt and distrust, which is sceptical. An enthusiastic or knowledgeable person would use them, and indifference would not amount to active refusal.

questions.s: Although the city is crowded, its ______ gardens offer visitors a peaceful escape.
questions.e: "Although" sets peaceful gardens against crowds: tranquil. Bustling, noisy and congested would not be escapes.

questions.s: His ______ for detail was legendary; he once noticed a single misplaced comma in a document of two hundred pages.
questions.e: Spotting one misplaced comma shows extreme attention to detail: fastidiousness. Indifference, carelessness and disdain mean the opposite.

questions.s: The professor's lecture was so ______ that students, unable to follow its tortuous reasoning, began to doubt their own competence.
questions.e: Reasoning students cannot follow, which damages their confidence, is hard to understand: abstruse. Trite means overused and obvious, which would be easy to follow.

questions.s: The more she ______ the problem, the less sure she was of any single solution.
questions.e: Growing uncertainty comes from looking more closely: examined. Forgetting or ignoring would not add doubts, and simplifying would reduce them.

questions.s: Sana's ______ determination to finish her degree impressed everyone, since she studied while working two jobs.
questions.e: Studying while holding two jobs shows determination that does not weaken: unwavering. Fleeting or reluctant determination would not produce such effort.

questions.s: Hamza's ______ nature meant he rarely spoke at gatherings and preferred to listen.
questions.e: Someone who rarely speaks and prefers listening is reticent. Boisterous and gregarious people are noisy and sociable, and arrogance is not implied by silence.

questions.s: Her ______ approach to problems, always asking "what if?", led to several creative solutions.
questions.e: Asking "what if" shows curiosity: inquisitive. Passive, careless and dismissive attitudes would not generate creative solutions.

questions.s: The ______ child hid behind her mother when the stranger approached.
questions.e: Hiding behind the mother shows shyness. Bold, rude and noisy children would not hide.

questions.s: The sudden loud noise made the horse ______ and run away from the road.
questions.e: A frightened horse running off is said to bolt. The other verbs make no sense with a horse running from a noise.

questions.s: The patient's condition, once thought ______, took an unexpected turn for the better, astonishing the doctors who had ______ his recovery.
questions.e: An unexpected improvement astonishes those who thought recovery impossible: hopeless ... doubted. Curable ... predicted would not produce astonishment.

questions.s: The weather was so ______ that the match had to be played in three separate sessions.
questions.e: Repeated interruptions suggest changeable weather: unpredictable. Stable and pleasant would not interrupt play.

questions.s: The ______ aroma of fresh bread filled the kitchen and made everyone hungry.
questions.e: Something that makes people hungry is tempting. A foul or bitter smell would not.

questions.s: It is ______ to cross the railway track when a train is approaching.
questions.e: Crossing in front of a train is a threat to life: dangerous. Pleasant, useful and permitted do not fit.

questions.s: The new employee was ______ to learn and soon mastered the software.
questions.e: Mastering software quickly goes with enthusiasm to learn. Unwilling and reluctant contradict this, and slow contradicts "soon".

questions.s: Usman was ______ to learn that he had won first prize, as he had not expected to place at all.
questions.e: Winning when he expected nothing causes surprise: astonished. Disappointed, bored and angry are negative or flat reactions that do not fit a pleasant, unexpected win.

questions.s: The minister's ______ manner, so unlike the warmth of his predecessor, made visitors feel they were intruding.
questions.e: "So unlike the warmth" signals coldness and distance: aloof. Affable, convivial and gregarious all describe friendliness and would not make visitors feel unwelcome.

questions.s: Alia's ______ shyness vanished as soon as she began to talk about her favourite subject.
questions.e: Shyness that vanishes once she starts speaking was present at the beginning: initial. Permanent shyness would not vanish.

questions.s: The manager was known to be ______ in public but ______ in private, praising staff in meetings and criticising them afterwards.
questions.e: Praise in meetings is gracious public behaviour, and criticism afterwards is harsh private behaviour, so "gracious ... harsh" matches. Reversing the pair swaps the two settings, and the other pairs do not describe praise and criticism.

questions.s: Her ______ smile put the nervous candidates at ease before the interview began.
questions.e: Putting nervous people at ease needs a friendly smile: warm. Cold or mocking smiles would increase nerves.

questions.s: The historian warned that the memoir, though vivid, was ______ source, since its author had a strong motive to ______ his own role.
questions.e: A strong personal motive makes the memoir partisan, and the natural bias is to exaggerate his own importance. "Impartial" and "neutral" contradict the warning, and "reliable" would not need warning.

questions.s: She was too ______ to accept help, even when the task was clearly beyond her strength.
questions.e: Refusing help despite clear need suggests stubborn pride. Grateful people accept help, and weary or quick does not explain the refusal.

questions.s: The news that the exams were postponed brought ______ to the students who had not finished revising.
questions.e: Extra time helps unprepared students: relief. Anguish and regret are not natural responses to a delay that helps.

questions.s: The old judge was famed for his ______; no sentence he passed was ever criticised as either too harsh or too ______.
questions.e: Praise for fairness means he was just: equity, and not too lenient either. The harsh/light pairs repeat rather than balance the two extremes.

questions.s: Her ______ answer, delivered without any hesitation, convinced the panel that she knew the subject well.
questions.e: Answering without hesitation shows confidence. Evasive, rambling and tentative answers would not convince a panel of her knowledge.

questions.s: The mayor's speech was meant to ______ the angry crowd, but it only made them more furious.
questions.e: The word "meant" with "but" shows the aim failed: she wanted to pacify them. Provoke or incite would be the result, not the aim.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
URDU : LANGUAGE
questions.e: The link is 'member and its class': Urdu is a kind of language. Rose : Flower has the same link, since Rose is a kind of flower. The other pairs show different links: Candle : Wax (object and the material it is made of); Neglect : Decay (cause and effect); Kilogram : Mass (unit and the quantity it measures).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
TONGUE : TASTE
questions.e: The link is 'organ and its function': the tongue is the organ used to taste. Eye : See has the same link, since the eye is the organ used to see. The other pairs show different links: Bee : Hive (animal and its home); Feather : Light (thing and its typical quality); Lawyer : Client (professional and the person served).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
LAWYER : CLIENT
questions.e: The link is 'professional and the person served': a lawyer serves a client. Shopkeeper : Customer has the same link, since a shopkeeper serves a customer. The other pairs show different links: Early : Late (word and its antonym); Lemon : Sour (thing and its typical quality); Study : Knowledge (cause and effect).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
LION : ROAR
questions.e: The link is 'animal and its sound': the lion's call is the roar. Snake : Hiss has the same link, since the snake's call is the hiss. The other pairs show different links: Bird : Nest (animal and its home); Generous : Stingy (word and its antonym); Speedometer : Speed (measuring instrument and what it measures).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
HAPPY : GLAD
questions.e: The link is 'word and its synonym': happy and glad mean the same. Begin : Start has the same link, since begin and start mean the same. The other pairs show different links: Scales : Justice (symbol and what it stands for); Whistle : Referee (tool and its user); Rose : Flower (member and its class).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
SHOPKEEPER : CUSTOMER
questions.e: The link is 'professional and the person served': a shopkeeper serves a customer. Teacher : Student has the same link, since a teacher serves a student. The other pairs show different links: Actor : Stage (worker and workplace); Book : Read (object and what is done to it); Baker : Bread (maker and what he makes).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:

The other pairs show different links: Sculptor : Statue (maker and what he makes); Bird : Nest (animal and its home); Barometer : Pressure (measuring instrument and what it measures).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
SCARCE : PLENTIFUL
questions.e: The link is 'word and its antonym': scarce and plentiful are opposites. Generous : Stingy has the same link, since generous and stingy are opposites. The other pairs show different links: Gavel : Judge (tool and its user); Crown : Monarchy (symbol and what it stands for); Doctor : Patient (professional and the person served).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
BATON : CONDUCTOR
questions.e: The link is 'tool and its user': a baton is the tool of a conductor. Plough : Farmer has the same link, since a plough is the tool of a farmer. The other pairs show different links: Quick : Fast (word and its synonym); Puppy : Dog (young animal and its adult); Horse : Stable (animal and its home).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
ACTOR : STAGE
questions.e: The link is 'worker and workplace': an actor works at a stage. Clerk : Office has the same link, since a clerk works at an office. The other pairs show different links: Flag : Nation (symbol and what it stands for); Transparent : Opaque (word and its antonym); Page : Book (part and whole).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
LENIENT : STRICT
questions.e: The link is 'word and its antonym': lenient and strict are opposites. Transparent : Opaque has the same link, since transparent and opaque are opposites. The other pairs show different links: Bee : Hive (animal and its home); Candle : Wax (object and the material it is made of); Neglect : Decay (cause and effect).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
JUDGE : COURT
questions.e: The link is 'worker and workplace': a judge works at a court. Chef : Kitchen has the same link, since a chef works at a kitchen. The other pairs show different links: Winter : Season (member and its class); Cobbler : Shoes (maker and what he makes); Ear : Hear (organ and its function).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
OPTIMIST : PESSIMIST
questions.e: The link is 'word and its antonym': optimist and pessimist are opposites. Rural : Urban has the same link, since rural and urban are opposites. The other pairs show different links: Rose : Flower (member and its class); Drought : Famine (cause and effect); Barometer : Pressure (measuring instrument and what it measures).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
CANDID : FRANK
questions.e: The link is 'word and its synonym': candid and frank mean nearly the same. Frugal : Thrifty has the same link, since frugal and thrifty mean nearly the same. The other pairs show different links: Petal : Flower (part and whole); Song : Sing (object and what is done to it); Plough : Farmer (tool and its user).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
ARDENT : PASSIONATE
questions.e: The link is 'word and its synonym': ardent and passionate mean nearly the same. Tranquil : Calm has the same link, since tranquil and calm mean nearly the same. The other pairs show different links: Heart : Pump (organ and its function); Foal : Horse (young animal and its adult); Actor : Stage (worker and workplace).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
WATT : POWER
questions.e: The link is 'unit and the quantity it measures': the watt is a unit of power. Metre : Length has the same link, since the metre is a unit of length. The other pairs show different links: Rose : Flower (member and its class); Day : Night (word and its antonym); Friction : Heat (cause and effect).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
COBBLER : SHOES
questions.e: The link is 'maker and what he makes': a cobbler makes shoes. Composer : Music has the same link, since a composer makes music. The other pairs show different links: Dislike : Hate (weaker and stronger degree of the same feeling or state); Dog : Kennel (animal and its home); Dog : Bark (animal and its sound).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
EXERCISE : FITNESS
questions.e: The link is 'cause and effect': exercise leads to fitness. Friction : Heat has the same link, since friction leads to heat. The other pairs show different links: Ring : Gold (object and the material it is made of); Shopkeeper : Customer (professional and the person served); Potter : Pot (maker and what he makes).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
FARMER : FIELD
questions.e: The link is 'worker and workplace': a farmer works at a field. Miner : Mine has the same link, since a miner works at a mine. The other pairs show different links: Cat : Meow (animal and its sound); Lawyer : Client (professional and the person served); Big : Large (word and its synonym).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
STUDY : KNOWLEDGE
questions.e: The link is 'cause and effect': study leads to knowledge. Drought : Famine has the same link, since drought leads to famine. The other pairs show different links: Conductor : Orchestra (leader and group led); Rural : Urban (word and its antonym); Dog : Bark (animal and its sound).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
CLOCK : TIME
questions.e: The link is 'measuring instrument and what it measures': a clock measures time. Barometer : Pressure has the same link, since a barometer measures pressure. The other pairs show different links: Study : Knowledge (cause and effect); Potter : Pot (maker and what he makes); Feather : Light (thing and its typical quality).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
CONDUCTOR : ORCHESTRA
questions.e: The link is 'leader and group led': a conductor leads an orchestra. Shepherd : Flock has the same link, since a shepherd leads a flock. The other pairs show different links: Hangar : Aeroplane (place and what it stores); Ruler : Length (measuring instrument and what it measures); Tired : Exhausted (weaker and stronger degree of the same feeling or state).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
FLAG : NATION
questions.e: The link is 'symbol and what it stands for': the flag is a symbol of nation. Crown : Monarchy has the same link, since the crown is a symbol of monarchy. The other pairs show different links: Petal : Flower (part and whole); Lung : Breathe (organ and its function); Tadpole : Frog (young animal and its adult).

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
TACITURN : GARRULOUS
questions.e: The link is antonyms: a taciturn person says little, a garrulous one says too much. Frugal and extravagant are opposites in the same way. Cautious and circumspect are synonyms, and the others pair a word with its related noun.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
EPHEMERAL : TRANSIENT
questions.e: The link is synonyms: ephemeral and transient both mean lasting a very short time. Pragmatic and practical also mean the same. Eminent and obscure, and benign and malignant, are opposites.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
THRIFTY : MISERLY
questions.e: The link is a good quality and its excessive form: thrift taken too far becomes miserliness, confidence taken too far becomes arrogance. Wealthy and rich, careful and cautious, and generous and charitable are synonyms.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
ANACHRONISM : TIME
questions.e: The link is an error and what it concerns: an anachronism puts something in the wrong time, a misnomer gives something the wrong name. An epilogue is part of a book, a villain opposes a hero, and rumour and gossip are synonyms.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
FLORIST : BOUQUET
questions.e: The link is a craftsman and what he produces: a florist arranges a bouquet, a cartographer draws a map. A lawyer works in court, a shepherd tends a flock and a gardener uses a spade.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
LIMB : AMPUTATE
questions.e: The link is a part and the action of cutting it away: a limb is amputated, a branch is pruned. Spin, fly and shine describe what a wheel, bird and gold do, not something done to cut them off.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
AUSTERITY : LUXURY
questions.e: The link is antonyms: austerity is a plain, strict way of life, and luxury is the opposite. Candour (frankness) and deceit are also opposites. Courage and bravery are synonyms, and the rest are unrelated pairs.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
ELEGY : POEM
questions.e: The link is a kind and its class: an elegy is a kind of poem, a biography is a kind of book. A chapter is a part of a book, an author makes it, and a library stores it.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
DEFAMATION : REPUTATION
questions.e: The link is a wrong act and what it damages: defamation harms a person's reputation, vandalism harms property. Punishment follows crime, a witness gives testimony, and an archaeologist studies ruins.

questions.s:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as:
SEISMOLOGIST : EARTHQUAKE
questions.e: The link is a scientist and what he studies: a seismologist studies earthquakes, a meteorologist studies weather. A jockey races on a racecourse, a sculptor uses a chisel and a choreographer directs dancers.

questions.s:
