questions.s: Which of the following would the author most likely agree with?
o: Every home should use the same method.
The choice of storage should suit local conditions.
Cost does not matter when choosing.
questions.e: The conclusion says the plan should be chosen according to local conditions, cost and habits.

questions.s: What is the passage mainly concerned with?
o: The invention of the tape recorder and its effect on valley life
The problem of preserving oral songs without making them rigid
The disappearance of weddings in the villages of the valleys
The best singers of the valley
questions.e: The author discusses how recording helps but may fix a changing tradition.

questions.s: According to the passage, why did versions of a song differ?
o: Singers were careless about the words they had learned
Collectors changed them when they wrote them down
Singers adjusted words and verses to suit occasions
The songs were too long to remember in full
questions.e: The passage says the changes were not carelessness but a way of keeping songs alive.

questions.s: What did some collectors do to avoid making a song seem fixed?
o: Recorded the same song from several singers
questions.e: The text says they recorded several singers and kept all versions.

questions.s: What worry do other collectors have?
o: People may copy recordings and stop changing songs
Recordings are too costly for most village singers
Songs may become too short to be worth singing
Singers will forget the weddings where songs are sung
questions.e: They fear the habit of change will fade as people copy recordings.

questions.s: The word 'preserves' in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.e: A recording keeps one performance exactly as it was.

questions.s: Which statement best reflects the author's final position?
o: Recording should be avoided altogether because it makes every song seem fixed.
Oral traditions are less valuable than the ones that are written down.
Songs should be changed as little as possible once they are recorded.
Recording is necessary, but it must be done without freezing the tradition.
questions.e: The author says lost songs cannot be recovered, so the issue is how to record without freezing the tradition.

questions.s: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Careless use of antibiotics encourages resistant bacteria.
questions.e: The passage explains how overuse leads to resistance and why careful use matters.

questions.s: According to the passage, how does resistance arise?
o: Bacteria learn to avoid doctors and the drugs they prescribe
Viruses turn into bacteria when the body is weak
Antibiotics slowly lose their strength when they are kept in storage
Tougher bacteria survive and multiply when drugs are used often
questions.e: Weak bacteria die and the stronger ones multiply in their place.

questions.s: According to the passage, what makes resistance worse?
o: Taking antibiotics for illnesses they cannot cure
Keeping antibiotics in a cool and dry place
Asking a doctor before using any antibiotic
Searching for new drugs in the laboratory
questions.e: The passage says resistance is made worse when people take antibiotics for illnesses they cannot cure or without a doctor's advice.

questions.s: Why are antibiotics no use for a common cold?
o: A cold is caused by a virus
Colds are too mild to need any drug
Antibiotics work only at night, when the body rests
Colds are caused by fungi in the nose
questions.e: The passage says antibiotics do not work against viruses.

questions.s: The word 'resource' in the final sentence suggests that antibiotics
o: can be used up in effectiveness if they are wasted
questions.e: Calling them a limited resource means misuse reduces their reliability.

questions.s: What can be inferred from the passage about new drugs?
o: They already exist for every kind of infection
They are unnecessary if people use antibiotics with care
They will not solve the problem quickly
They are cheaper than the old drugs
questions.e: The passage says finding new drugs takes years, so careful use is the practical defence for now.

questions.s: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: The Silk Road was a single paved highway built by one ruler across Asia.
The Silk Road was a network of routes along which goods and ideas travelled.
Silk was the only good that was traded along the routes between east and west.
Merchants usually travelled the whole length of the routes.
questions.e: The passage corrects the single-highway image and stresses relay trade and exchange of ideas.

questions.s: According to the passage, how did most goods travel?
o: One merchant carried them all the way
They were passed from trader to trader
They were sent by sea only
questions.e: The text says few merchants travelled the whole distance and goods changed hands many times.

questions.s: Which of the following is mentioned as moving along the routes?
questions.e: The passage lists spices, paper, glass, horses and metalwork, but not the others.

questions.s: Why did cities such as Samarkand and Kashgar grow rich?
o: They stood where routes met and served as markets
They controlled all of the silk production in China
They were ports that received ships from the west
They avoided paying fees to the rulers around them
questions.e: The passage says they were at meeting points of routes.

questions.s: Why do historians now use the term 'Silk Road' cautiously?
o: It is a modern word with no meaning at all
Silk was never traded along any of the routes
The routes were short and ran in a straight line
It can hide the variety of the trade
questions.e: The passage states the term can hide how varied the trade was.

questions.s: The author's attitude toward the term 'Silk Road' is
o: balanced: it is imperfect but still useful
questions.e: The author notes its limits yet says the picture remains a useful way to understand influence.

questions.s: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
o: Volunteers should always be paid, since their work should never be free labour.
Volunteering benefits givers as well as receivers, if it is well organised.
Only retired people make good volunteers for any charity.
Charities do not need volunteers if they have trained staff.
questions.e: The passage shows two-way benefit and says organisations must treat volunteers well.

questions.s: According to the passage, what might a student learn at a hospital reception?
o: To treat serious illnesses in the wards
To manage a charity from the front desk
To teach arithmetic to children after school
To speak calmly to frightened people
questions.e: The passage gives this as a skill classrooms do not quite teach.

questions.s: How does volunteering help a neighbourhood function, according to the passage?
o: It raises the price of property
It builds trust among people who would not otherwise meet
questions.e: The passage links mixing of ages and backgrounds to trust.

questions.s: What does the author warn against?
o: Giving time to charity every single week
Thanking volunteers for the work they have done
questions.e: The author says benefits should not be an excuse to treat volunteers as free labour.

questions.s: The word 'sincerely' in the passage means
questions.e: To thank someone sincerely is to do so genuinely.

questions.s: What can be inferred about a volunteer left without guidance?
o: The volunteer will always succeed without any guidance
The charity will save money on training
The experience may be frustrating for all concerned
The volunteer will be paid for the trouble
questions.e: The passage says it can be frustrating for everyone.

questions.s: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Trees damage cities more than they help.
Urban trees cool cities, but they must be chosen and cared for with thought.
Parks are always hotter than streets.
questions.e: The passage explains how trees cool and what makes planting succeed.

questions.s: According to the passage, why do crowded districts stay warm after dark?
o: The trees along the road give out warmth at night
Streetlights heat the air all night
Buildings are painted in dark colours
questions.e: Concrete and asphalt soak up heat and give it back slowly.

questions.s: In what two ways do trees reduce heat?
o: By casting shade and releasing water vapour
By blocking the wind and holding the soil in place
By storing heat and shedding their leaves
By drawing up water and warming their roots
questions.e: The passage names shade and release of water vapour.

questions.s: The comparison to sweat cooling skin is used to explain
o: how water vapour from trees cools the air
questions.e: Water vapour cools the air, much as sweat cools skin.

questions.s: Which practice do successful councils follow?
o: Planting the tallest trees possible along every road
Choosing local species and involving residents
Avoiding any watering once the saplings are planted
Replacing all of the trees every single year
questions.e: The passage states they choose local species and involve residents.

questions.s: What does the final sentence suggest about the benefits of planting trees?
o: They take time to appear but last long.
They appear within a week of planting.
They end after a few years of growth.
They are small and unimportant to the city.
questions.e: Benefits arrive slowly but last for decades.

questions.s: What is the central message of the passage?
o: Weavers in the nineteenth century gained from looms at once.
Automation changes jobs rather than simply ending them, so people need help to adapt.
questions.e: The passage argues that jobs shift and that support for adapting decides the outcome.

questions.s: According to the passage, what happened after mechanical looms spread?
o: Cloth became cheaper and new kinds of jobs appeared
No jobs were lost and no worker suffered any hardship
Cloth became more expensive as demand for it grew
All of the weavers became machine engineers
questions.e: The passage reports cheaper cloth, growth in demand and new jobs, along with real hardship for weavers.

questions.s: What does the example of 'a weaver of fifty' illustrate?
o: Weavers are the best people to become engineers
Older workers prefer machines to hand weaving
Moving into new work is not easy for everyone
Training is unnecessary for people of that age
questions.e: The author uses it to show that workers cannot always easily move into new jobs.

questions.s: Which of the following does the author say can decide whether automation brings widespread benefit?
o: Training, savings and support for those who must move
questions.e: These three are listed in the text.

questions.s: The word 'livelihoods' means
o: places of residence near the factories
questions.e: Hand weavers who lost their livelihoods lost their way of earning money.

questions.s: What attitude toward new machines does the author recommend?
o: Total resistance to every new machine that is built
Neither blind welcome nor resistance, but preparation
Total acceptance of every new machine without question
Complete indifference to what machines may bring
questions.e: The last sentence rejects both extremes and urges preparation.

questions.s: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: A kameti is useful only for weddings.
A kameti helps families save through mutual trust, but it carries a risk.
questions.e: The passage describes how it works and then names its weakness.

questions.s: How is the order in which members take the pot usually decided?
o: By the size of each family in the group
By the amount that each member has paid
By a bank manager at the start of the year
questions.e: The order is fixed at the start, often by drawing lots.

questions.s: Why does the kameti act as a discipline?
o: The money leaves the house before it can be spent elsewhere
Members are fined heavily if they are even a day late each month
A bank holds the money until it is needed
The pot is paid out in small sums each week
questions.e: The text says the money has left the house before it can be spent elsewhere.

questions.s: What disadvantage does the last member face?
o: Receiving a smaller pot than the first member received
Paying more each month than the other members
Having lent to others for months without reward
Being excluded from the group in later rounds
questions.e: The passage states the last member lends to the others without reward.

questions.s: The word 'defaulter' in the passage refers to someone who
o: fails to pay what is owed
questions.e: A member who fails to pay is a defaulter.

questions.s: Why do careful groups choose members with care?
o: They want the largest possible group of members
A defaulter can damage the whole circle
They wish to earn interest on the money
They must obey the rules of a bank
questions.e: The passage says a defaulter can damage the whole circle.

questions.s: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Tides are caused chiefly by the Moon's pull, with some effect from the Sun.
Tides are caused by the wind blowing steadily across the open sea and coast.
The Sun is the main cause of tides in most parts of the world.
Tides occur only in narrow bays where the water is squeezed.
questions.e: The passage explains the Moon as the main cause and then the Sun and shape of the coast.

questions.s: According to the passage, how many high tides do most coasts experience in a little over a day?
questions.e: Bulges on both sides of the Earth give two highs and two lows.

questions.s: Why is the Sun's effect on tides smaller than the Moon's?
o: It is smaller than the Moon in every way
It does not pull on water at all
It is hidden at night for most coasts
questions.e: The passage says its greater distance makes the effect smaller.

questions.s: When are the tides at their highest and lowest?
o: When the Moon is at right angles to the Sun
When the Sun and Moon are lined up with the Earth
questions.e: Aligned pulls combine, giving the most extreme tides.

questions.s: The word 'stranded' in the passage means
questions.e: A boat caught on the mud at low tide cannot move, i.e. is left aground.

questions.s: What does the passage suggest about narrow bays?
o: The tide never reaches them, even when it is at its highest
The tide can rise higher there than in open sea
The tide is weaker there than anywhere else
The Moon cannot be seen from inside them
questions.e: The water is squeezed, so the tide can rise much higher.

questions.s: What is the main message of the passage?
o: Everyone should read only difficult books.
Regular, enjoyable reading is a habit anyone can build.
Reading is possible only for those with free time.
questions.e: The passage says habit matters more than time, and enjoyment sustains it.

questions.s: According to the passage, what is the best way to begin?
o: Finishing one long book in the first week
Reading only at night when the house is quiet
Reading a small number of pages each day
Buying many books and arranging them on a shelf
questions.e: The passage suggests ten pages a day.

questions.s: Why does the author advise choosing enjoyable books?
o: Dull books may make a person give up reading
Enjoyable books are always shorter than dull ones
Impressive books are rare in most libraries
Dull books are cheaper than the enjoyable ones
questions.e: The text says forcing oneself through a dull book often leads to giving up.

questions.s: According to the passage, how does reading differ from short videos?
o: It trains the mind to follow an idea through many sentences
questions.e: The passage says reading trains attention in a way short videos do not.

questions.s: The word 'merely' in the passage means
questions.e: 'Merely seems impressive' means only seems impressive.

questions.s: What does the author think about putting a book aside?
o: It is a failure that a serious reader should always avoid
It is forbidden unless the book has been finished
It should be done after reading one page only
It is sensible when the book fails to interest you
questions.e: The author calls it a sensible choice, not a failure.

questions.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How the prepaid stamp and railways changed the post
How telephones were invented and then spread to villages
Why people stopped sending parcels through the post
How coaches were built for carrying the mail
questions.e: The passage traces the effect of the stamp and railways on the post.

questions.s: What was the usual practice before the prepaid stamp?
o: The sender paid with a coin
The receiver often paid on delivery
questions.e: The passage says the receiver often paid on delivery.

questions.s: According to the passage, what did railways allow?
o: Cheaper stamps for letters sent over long distances
Faster carriage of mail and sorting on the train
questions.e: The text says railways carried mail quickly and sorting could happen on the train.

questions.s: Which additional service did the post office offer in the Indian subcontinent?
o: Teaching reading to the village children
Sending money and saving small sums
Carrying passengers between villages by coach
questions.e: The passage mentions sending money and saving small sums.

questions.s: The word 'institution' in the passage most nearly means
questions.e: The post office became a trusted, lasting public body.

questions.s: What does the final sentence imply?
o: Stamps were unimportant to the people who wrote letters
A small change can have large social effects
The post will soon disappear altogether
questions.e: The author says a simple change such as the stamp can alter habits of a whole society.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The (A) number of (B) students (C) in the class (D) are forty.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). 'The number' is the subject and is singular, so the verb is 'is forty'. 'Students' only completes the phrase after 'of'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Please submit the form until Friday.
Please submit the form till by Friday.
Please submit the form on till Friday.
Please submit the form by Friday.
questions.e: 'By' marks a deadline for a single action; 'until' describes how long a situation continues. The other options pile up prepositions.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? She (A) congratulated (B) me (C) for (D) my success.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). We congratulate someone 'on' something, not 'for' it.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? He (A) entered (B) into (C) the room (D) quietly.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). 'Enter' is followed directly by its object: 'entered the room'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The number of vehicles crossing the bridge have increased.
A number of vehicles crossing the bridge has increased.
The numbers of vehicles crossing the bridge has increased.
The number of vehicles crossing the bridge has increased.
questions.e: 'The number' is singular and takes has; 'a number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb. The plural noun 'vehicles' is only the object of 'of', so it does not decide the verb.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: He likes swimming, to cycle and playing chess.
He likes swimming, cycling and to play chess.
He likes swim, cycling and playing chess.
He likes swimming, cycling and playing chess.
questions.e: Items in a list must have the same grammatical form. Here all three are -ing forms; mixing -ing with 'to' infinitives breaks parallelism.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The scissors is on the table.
The scissor are on the table.
The scissors are on the table.
A scissors are on the table.
questions.e: 'Scissors' is a plural-only noun for a tool with two blades, so it takes are, and it cannot take 'a'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The principal is angry from the late students.
The principal is angry for the late students.
The principal is angry at to the late students.
The principal is angry with the late students.
questions.e: 'Angry with' is used for a person; the other prepositions do not collocate with 'angry' in this meaning.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The rain has been falling since morning.
The rain is falling since morning.
The rain has been fall since morning.
The rain have been falling since morning.
questions.e: An action that began in the past and continues now needs the present perfect continuous: has been falling. 'Rain' is singular, and the verb after 'been' needs -ing.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? I have (A) much (B) friends (C) in (D) Lahore.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). 'Friends' is countable, so the word should be 'many'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The children (A) was (B) playing (C) in the (D) garden.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). 'Children' is plural, so the verb must be 'were'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The lecture, which lasted two hours, was informative.
The lecture, that lasted two hours, was informative.
The lecture, whom lasted two hours, was informative.
The lecture, which lasting two hours, was informative.
questions.e: A clause that only adds extra information, set off by commas, uses 'which' (not 'that'). 'Whom' is for people, and the clause needs a finite verb (lasted).

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? A number of (A) students (B) was (C) absent (D) yesterday.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb: 'were absent'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? (A) I am agree (B) with you (C) on this point (D) completely.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). 'Agree' is a verb, so it cannot follow 'am'. The correct form is 'I agree'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? There (A) were (B) only (C) two (D) book on the shelf.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). After 'two' the noun must be plural: 'books'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The teacher gave (A) Bilal and I (B) some (C) homework (D) yesterday.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). The pronoun is the object of 'gave', so it should be 'Bilal and me'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The price of (A) these oranges (B) are (C) too high (D) for me.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). The subject is 'the price', which is singular, so the verb should be 'is'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The water in these wells are not fit for drinking.
The water in these wells is not fit to drinking.
The water in these wells is not fit for drinking.
The water in these wells is not fitting for drink.
questions.e: 'Water' is singular, and 'fit for' is followed by a noun or an -ing form. The pattern 'fit to' takes a base verb, not 'drinking'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? We (A) had (B) better (C) to (D) go now.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). 'Had better' is followed by the base verb with no 'to'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Hardly nobody visited the garden in winter.
Hardly anyone did not visit the garden in winter.
Hardly no one visited the garden in winter.
Hardly anyone visited the garden in winter.
questions.e: 'Hardly' already has a negative meaning, so a second negative (nobody, no one, not) makes a double negative. 'Anyone' is correct.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: There is few sugar left in the jar.
There are little sugar left in the jar.
There is a few sugar left in the jar.
There is little sugar left in the jar.
questions.e: 'Sugar' is uncountable, so 'little' is correct with the singular verb is. 'Few' is for countable nouns.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? (A) Scarcely (B) had he left (C) than (D) the phone rang.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). 'Scarcely' pairs with 'when', not 'than'. 'No sooner' is the one that pairs with 'than'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? He is (A) good (B) in (C) Mathematics (D) and Physics.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). The usual collocation is 'good at'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Neither Hina nor Sana (A) have (B) finished (C) the (D) exercise yet.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). With 'neither … nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'Sana', which is singular: 'has finished'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Hamza (A) insisted (B) on (C) to pay (D) the bill.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). After a preposition the verb takes -ing: 'insisted on paying'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
questions.e: 'Honest' begins with a silent h, so it sounds like a vowel and takes 'an'. Singular countable nouns also need an article, and the word order must be subject, verb, complement.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? There (A) is (B) many (C) books (D) on the shelf.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). 'Books' is plural, so the verb should be 'are'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? I saw (A) an (B) one-eyed (C) man (D) in the bazaar.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). 'One' begins with the consonant sound 'w', so the article is 'a one-eyed man'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
questions.e: 'Afraid of' is the fixed collocation. 'From', 'with' and 'at' are not used after 'afraid' with an object like this.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? She (A) didn't (B) went (C) to (D) school today.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). After 'didn't' the verb returns to its base form: 'didn't go'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: She gave me some good advices.
She gave me a good advice.
She gave me some good advice.
questions.e: 'Advice' is uncountable: it has no plural and no 'a'. 'Advise' is the verb.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Ali (A) and (B) Bilal (C) are (D) cousin.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). The subject is plural, so the complement must be plural: 'cousins'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: I would have called you if I would have known your number.
I will have called you if I had known your number.
I would have called you if I had known your number.
I had called you if I knew your number.
questions.e: A third conditional uses the past perfect in the if-clause and 'would have' plus the participle in the main clause. 'Would have' never goes in the if-clause.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Ali is (A) a best student (B) in (C) our (D) class.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). A superlative takes 'the': 'the best student'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: He asked me where was I going.
He asked me where am I going.
He asked me where I were going.
He asked me where I was going.
questions.e: A reported question uses statement word order (subject before verb) and shifts the tense back: where I was going. 'Were' is only for 'you', 'we' and 'they' in this tense, or for the subjunctive.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The sun (A) rise (B) in the east (C) and sets (D) in the west.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). The subject 'sun' is singular, so the verb takes -s: 'rises'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The news about the results are encouraging.
The news about the results is encouraging.
The news about the results were encouraging.
The news about the results is encourage.
questions.e: 'News' looks plural but is uncountable and takes a singular verb. The adjective is 'encouraging'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Bilal is (A) one of (B) the best (C) player (D) in our school.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). After 'one of the' the noun must be plural: 'players'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: There are many people in the canteen.
There is many people in the canteen.
There are much people in the canteen.
There be many people in the canteen.
questions.e: The verb agrees with the plural noun 'people' (are), and 'many' is used with countable nouns, not 'much'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Aamna (A) and her (B) sisters (C) goes (D) to school by bus.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). The subject 'Aamna and her sisters' is plural, so the verb should be 'go'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Neither of (A) the boys (B) who came (C) were able (D) to solve the problem.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). 'Neither' is singular, so the verb should be 'was able'. 'Boys' and 'came' are correct as they stand.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Karachi is (A) the (B) most largest (C) city (D) in Pakistan.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). 'Largest' is already a superlative, so 'most' is not needed.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? This is the house (A) in which (B) my father (C) were (D) born.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). The singular subject 'my father' takes 'was', not 'were'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: I wish I would have checked my pocket earlier.
I wish I have checked my pocket earlier.
I wish I checked my pocket earlier.
I wish I had checked my pocket earlier.
questions.e: A wish about the past takes the past perfect (had checked). 'Would have' is not used after 'wish' for a past regret, and the simple past would refer to the present.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The old building, together with its gardens, were sold last year.
The old building, together with its gardens, was sold last year.
The old building, together with its gardens, has sold last year.
The old building, together with its gardens, is sold last year.
questions.e: 'Together with' does not make the subject plural, so the verb agrees with 'building' (singular). The building was the thing sold, so a passive verb in the past (was sold) is needed.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The (A) more (B) you practise, (C) better (D) you will become.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). The double comparative 'the more … the better' needs 'the' in both halves: 'the better you will become'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? (A) If I was (B) you, I would (C) start (D) preparing today.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). A wish or imagined situation in formal English uses the subjunctive 'were' for every person: 'If I were you'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The students (A) forgot (B) there (C) books (D) in the hall.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). The possessive is 'their'; 'there' refers to a place.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: I bought some furnitures for my new flat.
I bought a furniture for my new flat.
I bought some furniture for my new flat.
I bought many furniture for my new flat.
questions.e: 'Furniture' is uncountable, so it has no plural form and cannot take a, an or many. 'Some' is fine with uncountable nouns.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If it rained tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If it rains tomorrow, we would stay at home.
questions.e: A real future condition takes the present simple in the if-clause and will in the main clause. Will is never used in the if-clause here, and the tenses must not be mixed.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? (A) She don't (B) like (C) tea (D) without sugar.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). With a third person singular subject the negative auxiliary is doesn't, so the form should be 'She doesn't'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Although (A) it was raining, (B) but (C) we (D) went out for a walk.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). 'Although' and 'but' both join clauses, so only one may be used. Remove 'but'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Please (A) accept (B) my (C) advise (D) and rest.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). The noun is 'advice'; 'advise' is the verb.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? By the time we (A) arrived, (B) the film (C) has (D) started.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). Of two past actions the earlier takes the past perfect: 'had started'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Walking to school, a stray dog barked at Bilal.
Walking to school, a stray dog was barking Bilal.
Walking to school, Bilal was barked at by a stray dog.
Walked to school, a stray dog barked at Bilal.
questions.e: The opening phrase must describe the subject that follows. In the wrong options the dog seems to be walking to school, which is a dangling modifier; only in the correct option is Bilal the walker.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? You (A) should (B) to (C) take (D) more rest.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). Modal verbs such as 'should' are followed by the base verb without 'to'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The shop (A) opens (B) in (C) 9 a.m. (D) every day.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). Clock times take 'at': 'opens at 9 a.m.'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? I have (A) a (B) MBA degree (C) from (D) Punjab University.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). 'MBA' begins with the vowel sound 'em', so the article is 'an'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Aamir (A) has been working (B) in this office (C) since five years (D) and enjoys it.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). 'Since' needs a point in time. A length of time like 'five years' takes 'for', so the part should be 'for five years'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Please tell me (A) where is the post office (B) and (C) how (D) far it is.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). In an indirect question the verb follows the subject: 'where the post office is'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The man who's car was stolen reported it to the police.
The man whose car was stolen reported it to the police.
The man whom car was stolen reported it to the police.
The man which car was stolen reported it to the police.
questions.e: 'Whose' shows possession. 'Who's' means 'who is' or 'who has', 'whom' is an object form and 'which' is not used for people.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Hardly we had reached the platform when the train left.
Hardly had we reached the platform than the train left.
Hardly we reached the platform when the train had left.
Hardly had we reached the platform when the train left.
questions.e: 'Hardly' at the start of a sentence forces inversion (had we reached) and pairs with 'when', not 'than'. 'Than' belongs with 'no sooner'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The prize was shared between Hina and me.
The prize was shared between Hina and I.
The prize was shared among Hina and me.
The prize was shared between Hina and my.
questions.e: After a preposition the object form 'me' is used, even in a pair with another name. 'Among' is for more than two, and 'my' needs a noun after it.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Our teacher (A) explained (B) the lesson (C) very (D) clear.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). A word describing how the lesson was explained is an adverb: 'clearly'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Neither the manager (A) nor (B) his assistants (C) was ready (D) for the meeting.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). With 'neither … nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'assistants', which is plural: 'were ready'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Not only she passed, but she also topped the class.
Not only did she pass, but she also topped the class.
Not only did she passed, but she also topped the class.
Not only she did pass, but she also topped the class.
questions.e: A sentence beginning with 'not only' needs inversion with an auxiliary (did she), and the main verb returns to the base form (pass), because 'did' carries the tense.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? We (A) were (B) all (C) very (D) surprised for the news.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). We are surprised 'at' or 'by' something, not 'for'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? It (A) is (B) long time (C) since (D) I last saw him.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). The noun phrase needs an article: 'a long time'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The doctor advised him resting for a week.
The doctor advised him that rest for a week.
The doctor advised to him rest for a week.
The doctor advised him to rest for a week.
questions.e: 'Advise someone' is followed by 'to' plus the base verb. 'Advised him resting' and 'to him' are not grammatical.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Ayesha (A) and (B) me (C) went (D) to the market.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). As part of the subject, the pronoun should be in the subject form: 'Ayesha and I'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
questions.e: A finished time marker such as 'yesterday' needs the simple past. The present perfect cannot be used with a time that has ended.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? When I (A) reached (B) the station, (C) the train (D) already left.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). The train left before I arrived, so the earlier action needs the past perfect: 'had already left'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The (A) Sun (B) rises (C) in (D) east.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). Points of the compass used as a place take 'the': 'in the east'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Ayesha has lived in Lahore since 2015.
Ayesha has lived in Lahore for 2015.
Ayesha has lived in Lahore since ten years.
questions.e: 'Since' goes with a point in time and needs a perfect tense; 'for' goes with a length of time. 'Lives … since' mixes a simple present with a duration that began in the past.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The window (A) was (B) broke (C) by (D) a stone.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). A passive needs the past participle: 'was broken'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Rarely we do see such talent.
Rarely do we see such talent.
Rarely do we saw such talent.
questions.e: A negative or near-negative adverb such as 'rarely' at the start of a sentence causes inversion with an auxiliary (do we), and the main verb stays in the base form (see).

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Amir is taller than his brother.
Amir is more taller than his brother.
Amir is tall than his brother.
Amir is taller then his brother.
questions.e: Short adjectives take -er alone and never 'more' as well. The comparison word is 'than'; 'then' refers to time.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? He wants to become (A) doctor (B) and (C) serve (D) the poor.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). A singular job title needs an article: 'a doctor'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: This is the most best book that I have ever read.
This is the best book that I have ever read.
This is best book that I have ever read.
This is the bestest book that I have ever read.
questions.e: 'Best' is already the superlative of 'good', so it takes no 'most' or -est, and it needs 'the'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Bilal borrowed me his notes before the test.
Bilal lend me his notes before the test.
Bilal lents me his notes before the test.
Bilal lent me his notes before the test.
questions.e: The giver lends; the receiver borrows. The past tense of 'lend' is 'lent', and 'borrowed me' is not grammatical.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The new library (A) has (B) a large (C) collection of (D) book.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). After 'collection of' the noun is plural: 'books'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Each of the students have borrowed a book.
Each of the students has borrowed a book.
Each of the student has borrowed a book.
Each of the students has borrow a book.
questions.e: Each is singular, so it takes has; after 'of the' the noun must be plural (students). 'Have' is tempting because 'students' is plural, but the subject is 'each'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Our teacher told us (A) to read, (B) to write (C) and (D) that we should revise.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). The list needs parallel forms: 'to read, to write and to revise'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Faisal (A) prefers (B) walking (C) than (D) driving.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). 'Prefer' takes 'to': 'prefers walking to driving'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The committee (A) comprising of (B) five members (C) met (D) on Monday.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). 'Comprise' means 'consist of' and is not followed by 'of'. The correct forms are 'comprising five members' or 'composed of five members'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Neither the teacher nor the students was aware of the change.
Neither the teacher nor the students is aware of the change.
Neither the teacher nor the students were aware of the change.
Neither the teacher or the students were aware of the change.
questions.e: With neither … nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'students', so it is plural (were). 'Neither' must be paired with 'nor', not 'or'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? They (A) have (B) been knowing (C) each other (D) for years.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). 'Know' is a stative verb and does not take the continuous; the correct form is 'have known'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The team has chosen it's captain.
The team has choose its captain.
The team has chosen its' captain.
The team has chosen its captain.
questions.e: 'Its' without an apostrophe is the possessive. 'It's' means 'it is' or 'it has', and 'its'' does not exist. The present perfect needs the past participle 'chosen'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The Indus is the longest river in Pakistan.
Indus is the longest river in Pakistan.
The Indus is longest river in Pakistan.
An Indus is the longest river in Pakistan.
questions.e: River names take 'the', and a superlative adjective also takes 'the'. 'An' is wrong because the name refers to one particular river.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? (A) The girl (B) who's (C) bag was stolen (D) complained to the guard.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). The possessive is 'whose'; 'who's' means 'who is' or 'who has'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The (A) quality of (B) the apples (C) are (D) excellent.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). The subject is 'the quality', which is singular, so the verb is 'is'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? She (A) hardly (B) never (C) misses (D) a class.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). 'Hardly' is already negative, so 'never' makes a double negative. The correct word is 'ever'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The (A) principal (B) along with (C) the teachers (D) were present.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). 'Along with' does not change the subject, which is the singular 'principal': 'was present'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? I am (A) looking forward (B) to see you (C) at the (D) wedding.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). In 'look forward to' the word 'to' is a preposition, so an -ing form follows: 'to seeing you'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The students were asked to bring there own equipment.
The students were asked to brought their own equipment.
The students were asked to bring theirs own equipment.
The students were asked to bring their own equipment.
questions.e: 'Their' is the possessive adjective; 'there' is an adverb of place, and 'theirs' is a pronoun that cannot be followed by a noun. After 'to' the verb takes its base form.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: He is used to waking up early.
He is used to wake up early.
He used to waking up early.
He is use to waking up early.
questions.e: 'Be used to' means 'be accustomed to' and is followed by an -ing form, because 'to' is a preposition. 'Used to' followed by the base verb describes a past habit and has no 'is'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: I look forward to meet you at the wedding.
I look forward to meeting you at the wedding.
I look forward for meeting you at the wedding.
I am looking forward to meet you at the wedding.
questions.e: In 'look forward to', the word 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by an -ing form. The infinitive 'to meet' is the common error.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Zahid (A) is (B) very (C) fond (D) about cricket.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). The adjective 'fond' is followed by 'of': 'fond of cricket'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? He is (A) married (B) with (C) a doctor (D) in Lahore.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). We are married 'to' someone, not 'with'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Two hundreds people were injured in the accident.
Two hundred of people were injured in the accident.
Two hundred people were injured in the accident.
Two hundred people was injured in the accident.
questions.e: After a definite number the word 'hundred' stays singular, with no 's' and no 'of'. 'People' is plural and takes were.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? She (A) has (B) been (C) teaching (D) here from 2015.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). With a perfect tense the starting point is introduced by 'since': 'since 2015'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: She prefers tea over than coffee.
She prefers more tea to coffee.
questions.e: 'Prefer' is followed by 'to', not 'than' (except when two infinitives or -ing forms are compared in some patterns). 'More' is redundant after 'prefer'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? My sister (A) is (B) teach (C) in (D) a school.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). After 'is' the verb needs -ing: 'is teaching'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? I (A) would (B) have (C) gone (D) if I knew about it.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). A third conditional needs the past perfect in the if-clause: 'if I had known'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? We are (A) looking (B) for (C) a solution (D) on this problem.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). The noun 'solution' takes 'to': 'a solution to this problem'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? They (A) is (B) going (C) to (D) the market.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). The plural subject 'they' needs 'are'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The boys (A) and girls (B) of this school (C) is (D) very polite.
questions.e: The error is in part (C). The compound subject 'boys and girls' is plural, so the verb should be 'are'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The train has left before we reached the station.
The train had left before we reached the station.
The train had left before we reaching the station.
The train had left before we have reached the station.
questions.e: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect (had left), and the later takes the simple past (reached). 'Has left' and 'have reached' mix in the present, and 'reaching' cannot follow 'we' without an auxiliary.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The price of mobile phones have risen.
The prices of the mobile phone has risen.
The price of mobile phones has risen.
The price of mobile phones are risen.
questions.e: The subject is 'the price', which is singular, so the verb is has risen. The plural 'phones' belongs to the phrase after 'of'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: Seldom does a student complete all the exercises.
Seldom a student completes all the exercises.
Seldom does a student completes all the exercises.
Seldom do a student complete all the exercises.
questions.e: 'Seldom' at the start of a sentence causes inversion with does, and the main verb returns to the base form (complete). 'Do' would not agree with the singular 'a student'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? The tea (A) is (B) too (C) hot (D) to drunk.
questions.e: The error is in part (D). After 'to' the verb takes its base form: 'to drink'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: He have not finished his work yet.
He has not finish his work yet.
He has not finished his work yet.
He has no finished his work yet.
questions.e: The present perfect needs has with a singular subject and the past participle 'finished'; the negative is 'not'.

questions.s: Which sentence is correct?
o: The bus has arrived ten minutes ago.
The bus arrived ten minutes ago.
The bus arrives ten minutes ago.
The bus was arrived ten minutes ago.
questions.e: 'Ago' marks a finished past time, so the simple past is required; the present perfect cannot be used with it. 'Arrive' is intransitive and has no passive.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? He (A) told to me (B) that (C) he was ill (D) yesterday.
questions.e: The error is in part (A). 'Tell' takes its object directly: 'told me'. 'Say' is the verb that takes 'to'.

questions.s: Which part of the sentence contains an error? Both of (A) my (B) brother (C) are (D) doctors.
questions.e: The error is in part (B). After 'both of my' the noun is plural: 'brothers'.
